name: Diego Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Diego. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We don't work for AI companies, employers, unions or any party. Everything you tell me is confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and, separately, what you really think. Could you start by telling me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Diego, 27, and I operate a dragline at a big open-cut phosphate mine. The phosphate goes into fertiliser. A dragline is a giant digging machine with a bucket on cables that strips the rock off the top of the ore, and ours weighs about as much as a ship. I'm one of four senior operators on it. I live on my own in a flat in town and I'm saving for a place of my own.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Twelve-hour shifts, two days, two nights, four off. I sit in the cab high up and swing the bucket out, drag it back through the dirt and dump it on the spoil pile, maybe sixty times an hour. It's all about timing and feel; the best operators move the most dirt with the least wear on the ropes. I love the rhythm. What I don't love is the four a.m. stretch on nights when your eyes go heavy.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'm going to describe five pictures of the future, one at a time. The first is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine by me. I like my job the way it is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'm not surprised, and that a few tools making paperwork quicker is fine. My brother works in IT in the city and he'd be the disappointed one. I'd send him a message just to wind him up.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, it means nothing much changes for me. Fertiliser's always needed, the mine has twenty years in the plan and I'm one of the best on the dragline. I'd feel pretty secure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep working and keep saving for the deposit, I've got about five months of expenses put away. I'd use the AI chat thing now and then, like I did last month to compare two mortgage offers. Otherwise, business as usual.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. Steady.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Anything that would worry you in that picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: House prices in town. They've gone up a lot since the expansion. If I don't buy in the next couple of years, I might not afford anything decent.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How did comparing the mortgage offers with the chat tool go?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It was handy, it laid the numbers out in a table. I still rang the bank to check, because I don't trust it completely. But it saved me an evening with a calculator.

say: He's **not surprised**, and quicker paperwork is fine.
He'd **wind up** his brother in IT, who'd be disappointed.
think: **Fertiliser** is always needed and the mine has **twenty years** planned.
Being among the best on the **dragline** makes him feel secure.
do: Keep working and saving for a **house deposit**.
Use the **AI chat tool** now and then for things like mortgage offers.
Carry on with **business as usual** at the mine.
S0.quote: Fertiliser's always needed, the mine has twenty years in the plan and I'm one of the best on the dragline.
fieldNote: **Secure job** and a long mine plan make him calm here.
His live worry is **house prices** rising in town.
Uses AI tools **practically** but double-checks with the bank.

steps.text: Keep running the dragline on the two-two-four roster
Keep saving for a house deposit in town

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Yeah, that sounds realistic. Some of it's already starting at our place.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's change, and we'll deal with it like we always do. I wouldn't be the guy shouting about robots. I'd also say the mine owes it to people to retrain them properly if their jobs go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think the office side gets hit first: the planners, the purchasing team, the people who write the shift reports. The dragline already has an auto-swing mode we use sometimes, and it'll get better. My job's safe for now, but I'd keep an eye on it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask to be trained on the new auto-swing system properly, so I'm the one who runs it. I'd keep saving, and I'd probably buy the house sooner rather than later, while my job's solid. I'd use the AI tools a bit more if the mine brings them in for reports.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little uneasy. More curious than scared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who at the mine would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Shelley in mine planning. She's brilliant, but her whole job is schedules and spreadsheets. If software does that, she's in more trouble than me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why buy the house sooner?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because banks like steady jobs. If the mine starts cutting, even people who keep their job look riskier on paper. I'd rather sign while I look solid.

say: It's change, and they'll **deal with it** as always.
The mine owes people **proper retraining** if their jobs go.
think: The **office side** gets hit first: planners, purchasing, report writers.
The dragline's **auto-swing mode** will improve, so he'll watch it.
do: Get properly trained on the **auto-swing system**.
Buy the **house sooner** while his job looks solid to the bank.
Use **AI tools** more if the mine brings them in for reports.
S1.quote: Banks like steady jobs. If the mine starts cutting, even people who keep their job look riskier on paper.
fieldNote: He clearly sees **desk jobs** at the mine as more exposed than his.
Thinks about **timing the mortgage** around how secure he looks.

steps.text: Get trained to run the dragline's auto-swing system
Buy a house in town while the job looks solid
Keep working his shifts on the dragline

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. That's a big jump.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I'll believe it when I see it, but I'd also say we need a plan, quick. I'm not a protest guy. I'd want the government and the company to sit down and work out what happens to towns like ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, the thinking AI part doesn't hit me in 2028, except the planners and supervisors around me go. But the robots in 2031, that's different. I'd be 31, and a dragline is a perfect job for a robot: same swing, all day, every day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd hold off on the house, because I don't want a mortgage on a job with three years left. I'd save hard, maybe get to nine months of expenses. And I'd start an electrical apprenticeship part-time, so I've got a trade that lasts a bit longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. Not falling apart, but worried.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why would an electrician last longer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Somebody has to install the robots, wire them, and fix them when they go wrong, at least at the start. I'm not saying forever. Just longer than me sitting in a cab.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said a dragline is a perfect job for a robot. Does that annoy you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A bit, yeah. People think it's just pulling levers. But I can't argue: a machine that never gets tired at four a.m. would do it well.

say: He'll believe it when he sees it, but wants a **plan quickly**.
Government and company should plan for **mining towns** together.
think: The **2028 AI** mainly removes planners and supervisors around him.
Robots in **2031** suit the dragline perfectly: same swing, all day.
do: **Hold off** on the house rather than borrow against three years.
Save up to **nine months** of expenses.
S2.quote: A dragline is a perfect job for a robot: same swing, all day, every day.
fieldNote: He admits his job is **easy to automate**, despite his pride in it.
Delays the **house** because three years is too short for a mortgage.
Moves toward a **trade** rather than a desk career.

steps.text: Put the house purchase on hold
Save up to nine months of expenses

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit more breathing room.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's time to sort this out if people stop arguing and start planning. I'd be in favour of the company and the government splitting the cost of retraining. I'd say that in the crib room, not on the internet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd have until about 2034 on the dragline. That's seven years, which is a decent run. I could get a trade and still buy a house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy a smaller place than I wanted, in the next couple of years, and pay it down hard. I'd do the electrical apprenticeship over three years while still working. And I'd stay on the dragline as long as they need me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Concerned, but okay. I've got a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a smaller house a hard choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I wanted a big shed for my motorbikes, but I can live without the shed. A small mortgage is better than a big one if I'm changing trades.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your brother in IT?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my brother he's in more trouble than me this time, and he'd hate hearing it. His coding job goes in 2031, mine in 2034.

Company and government should **split** the cost of retraining.
think: He'd have until about **2034** on the dragline.

Stay on the **dragline** as long as needed.
feel: **Concerned** but **okay**, because he has a plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. That's most of a career's worth of planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is plenty if people use it. I'd tell the younger operators to get a second ticket now. Most of them won't listen, but I'd say it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be fine, I think. I'd have the house, a trade and some savings by 2036. The dragline is a weird old machine, so it might be one of the last to get a robot fitted. I'd guess I'm safe until about 2039, maybe longer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd buy the house I actually want, with the shed. I'd do the electrical ticket over four or five years, no rush. And I'd think about renting out a room for extra income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Pretty calm. Just keeping an eye on things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could go wrong with that plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Prices for phosphate could drop and the mine could cut back, robots or not. That's happened before in this town. I'd still be okay with a trade.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ever leave mining by choice?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe in my late thirties, if the electrical side paid well. I'm not married to the dragline. I just like it.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because I'd have to drop the house and scramble for a trade at the same time. What would help is the mine paying for apprenticeships while we still work, and honest dates about when the machines are coming.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about pride. Running a dragline well is a skill, and it's strange to hear it might be easy for a robot. I'd want somebody to remember that people did this well once.

headlineQuote: Running a dragline well is a skill, and it's strange to hear it might be easy for a robot.
portrait: A 27-year-old **senior dragline operator** at an open-cut phosphate mine, single and saving for a house.
Pragmatic and **steady**; uses AI chat tools now and then but double-checks them.
Calm in AI Plateau, uneasy in Steady Disruption as **desk jobs** around him shrink.
In the AGI pictures, his plan is an **electrical trade** and a house timed to his job security.
Proud of his skill, yet admits a dragline is a **natural job** for a robot.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he'd drop the house and scramble for a trade.
whatWouldHelp: **Paid apprenticeships** while still working, and **honest dates** about the machines.
